title: Avalanche galleries on the Simplon road
place: Simplon pass road from Rothwald to the pass
summary: From Napoleon's road to the modern highway, roofs of stone and concrete were built over the Simplon road to let avalanches pass over it.
why: Below the Kaltwasser glacier the Simplon road crosses steep avalanche slopes. The engineer Céard wanted most of the road above Schallbett in tunnels and galleries (roofed road sections), so that it could be used in winter. Paris refused; only the Glacier gallery was built by 1805.

In the early 1830s the cantonal engineer Ignaz Venetz built more galleries: the Kaltwasser and the Josef gallery. The Josef gallery was rebuilt in 1852, and the Kaltwasser gallery was made longer shortly after 1869. Avalanches still destroyed the refuge house at the pass in 1903 and 1913.
The road was extended from the 1950s. The maps show long covered sections from 1970 and almost continuous galleries from Schallbett to the pass by 1995.
gained: Long galleries now cover most of the road between Rothwald and the pass. Not confirmed: how many days the road is open in winter thanks to them.
The old Glacier gallery with a piece of the old road survives as a monument.
lost: The Kaltwasser and Josef galleries and the tunnel at Schallbett disappeared in the modern road building.

title: Avalanche barriers on the Gurschen above Andermatt
place: Slope above the Gurschenwald (Bannwald), south of Andermatt
summary: Above the old protection forest of Andermatt, rows of avalanche barriers cover the starting zone; they grew after the deadly avalanche winter of 1951.
why: Avalanches from the Gurschen slope threaten Andermatt. A small old forest, the Bannwald, protects the village. Since about 1850 people planted trees around it and built barriers on the upper slope to help the young trees.
On 20 January 1951 avalanches killed 13 people in Andermatt. Houses and a hotel were destroyed. The winters of 1951 and 1975 brought avalanches into the village.
After 1951/52 and 1974/75 more planting and technical barriers followed. The map shows the barrier field growing between 1880 and 1980.
gained: A study by the WSL calculates that the barriers and the forest together prevent a wide destruction of Andermatt in a very rare (300-year) avalanche.
In the model about 3 people would be affected with the barriers and about 26 without them.
lost: 13 people died in Andermatt in January 1951 before the barriers were extended.
The open slope above the forest now carries rows of structures. Not confirmed: their cost and upkeep.

title: Schafberg barriers and Giandains dams, Pontresina
place: Schafberg (Munt da la Bês-cha) above Pontresina
summary: Pontresina has built avalanche walls on the Schafberg since 1882; in 2003 two large dams were built instead of barriers on thawing permafrost.
why: For centuries over 1,000 sheep grazed the Schafberg and reduced its forest. Before 1860 Pontresina had only a few old parts safe from avalanches. Between them, hotels were built in danger zones until about 1900.
From 1882 people built dry stone walls on the Schafberg. Planting went along with it. Today there are 624 structures with over 16 km of length.

Studies from 1988 found that the starting zone of Val Giandains lies on permafrost (ground that stays frozen all year). Barriers there would move, and debris flows were possible. So two offset catch dams were built below it, finished in 2003.
gained: The two dams, each 230 m long and 13.5 m high, can hold 240,000 m3 of avalanche snow and also debris flows.
The dams cost about a quarter of full barriers in the starting zone and replaced about 10 km of new barriers.
From 1953 to 1988, 3.73 million young trees were planted on the Schafberg.
lost: The dams needed the clearing of 2.1 ha of old forest and 1.0 ha of young forest.
The open slopes of the Schafberg now carry long rows of walls and steel structures.

title: Avalanche barriers and planting above Airolo
place: Slopes of the Pizzo Canariscio and the Vallascia basin above Airolo
summary: Airolo protected itself with stone walls from 1889; after the avalanche of 1951 (10 dead) and new near-misses it covered the starting zones with steel snow bridges and nets.
why: Avalanches from the slopes above Airolo hit the village in 1886, 1895, 1923 and 1951. From 1889 people built dry stone walls and terraces in the starting zones. These were low and had little effect.
On 12 February 1951 the avalanche of the Vallascia killed 10 people. After it about 5 km of permanent snow bridges were built and over 30 ha were planted.

In 1984 and 1986 snow again went over the protective wall and damaged houses. In 1986 the canton started a large project (first estimate 56 million francs) with steel snow bridges, nets, catch dams and planting.
gained: The first two stages strongly reduced the danger of large avalanches from the Vallascia, says the cantonal commission.
When finished, about 12 km of snow-holding structures stand above the village.
In the Dragoni valley a catch dam of 300 m length and 18 m height replaced barriers in a starting zone with landslide danger.
lost: 10 people died in 1951.
A large dam directly above the village was rejected, because it would mark the land and take a wide area of farmland.
Planting fell far short of the plan: about 42,000 young trees instead of 270,000.

title: Lammbach check dams above Brienz
place: Lammbach torrent, Brienz, Schwanden and Hofstetten
summary: After huge debris flows in 1894 and 1896, 22 stone check dams were built in the Lammbach gorge, the torrent was led to the lake between dams and the slopes above were reforested.
why: The Lammbach comes down from the Brienzer Rothorn to the lake. In May 1499 its debris flows destroyed the hamlet of Kienholz, and about 400 people died. In 1824 debris flows of the Lamm-, Schwander- and Glyssibach killed 6 people.

In 1894 and 1896 very large debris flows reached the lake and covered much of Kienholz. After 1896, 22 check dams were built in the gorge. Protective dams were built directly above the settled area, and on the upper slopes more than 8 million trees were planted and about 80,000 m3 of dry stone walls were built.
The old maps show the change on the fan. In 1890 the Lammbach ends on a bare gravel strip at Innere Ey, near Hofstetten. By 1920 it flows in a straight bed between dams towards the lake at Kienholz.
gained: No extraordinary debris flows happened in the 20th century. In 2005, when the nearby Glyssibach and Trachtbach caused disasters, the Lammbach stayed quiet, probably also because of the works.
In 2019 the Bern parliament agreed unanimously to new works for 18.8 million francs, among them a new sediment trap for 75,000 m3 and repairs of the old dams.
lost: Behind the old dams lies more than 1 million m3 of debris, and their storage space is used up. If the old dams fail in an extreme event, this debris can come down.
The gravel fan at Innere Ey, an open area of the torrent, became farmland and later houses. When and how this happened is not confirmed.

title: Avalanche barriers on the Schiahorn and Dorfberg, Davos
summary: After the avalanches of 1919 Davos built stone walls on the Schiahorn; after 1951 and 1968 steel barriers covered the starting zones on the Schiahorn and Dorfberg.
why: Avalanches from the Schiahorn and the Dorfberg threaten Davos Dorf. After heavy avalanches in 1919 Davos built large barriers of stone walls on both slopes in 1920–1924. At that time they were a model for all of Switzerland.

In 1951 Davos itself was spared. Later the SLF set up a test site for new structures on the Dorfberg. On 26 and 27 January 1968, 41 avalanches came down and killed 13 people in Davos. The largest started on the east flank of the Schiahorn, where about 5 km of barriers already stood.
After 1968 Davos added more barriers, an avalanche dam below the Schiahorn and road galleries. Today about 21 km of barriers and four galleries protect Davos.
gained: The town is protected by about 21 km of permanent barriers and four road galleries.
In 1951 the new barriers kept the avalanches away from the town.
The Dorfberg became a test site where the SLF compared new snow bridges with old walls.
lost: The open mountain slopes above Davos now carry rows of walls and steel structures. Old walls along the fall line still stand next to the newer ones.
The barriers did not stop the disaster of 1968: 13 people died in Davos.

title: Avalanche winter 1951 and the start of modern avalanche protection
place: Swiss Alps; worst in Vals, Andermatt and Airolo
summary: In the winter of 1950/51 avalanches killed 98 people in Switzerland; after it, the federal state paid much more for steel barriers, planting and research.
why: In January and February 1951 very much snow fell in the Alps. From 18 January it snowed for 88 hours without a break. About 1,500 buildings were destroyed and 98 people died.
The worst places were Vals (19 dead on 20 January), Andermatt (13 dead on the same day) and Airolo (10 dead on 12 February). In Graubünden alone 54 people died.

Until then walls and terraces of stone were the main protection in the starting zones (the slopes where avalanches begin). On 19 December 1951 the federal parliament passed a law with higher federal subsidies (money from the state) for planting and barriers. The SLF in Davos (the federal snow and avalanche institute, founded in 1942) tested new structures. Steel snow bridges and nets became the standard. The first guidelines came in 1955.
gained: Since 1951 about 2 billion francs went into avalanche protection works. In Graubünden alone about 250 km of barriers were built in 50 years.
Planting of protection forest went together with barriers. Experts said: no barriers without new forest. By area, forest is the most important protection.
Hazard maps (maps that show where avalanches can reach) now exist for almost all settlements.
The SLF grew from a snow laboratory on the Weissfluhjoch (1936) into the national centre for avalanche research and the avalanche warning service.
lost: 98 people died in the winter of 1950/51, and about 1,500 buildings were destroyed.
The barriers need care for ever. Graubünden says that maintenance becomes a permanent task.
The root problem was older: many mountain forests had been overused or cleared, and grazing stopped young trees from growing.

title: Illgraben check dams and debris-flow station
place: Illgraben above Susten (Leuk), between the Pfynwald and the village
summary: After a large rockfall in 1961, a big retention wall and 28 check dams were built in the Illgraben, one of the most active debris-flow torrents of the Alps; since 2000 WSL measures its debris flows.
why: The Illgraben runs from the Illhorn (2716 m) to the Rhone (610 m). Several debris flows (fast flows of mud and stones) come down every year. The village of Susten stands on the torrent's fan, and large debris flows put it in danger.

In 1961 a rock slide of about 3.5 million m3 fell in the catchment. After this, debris flows became more frequent. From 1967 to 1969 a large retention wall was built in the middle part of the gorge, and the channel below it down to the Rhone was held with 28 more check dams (Sperren, walls across the stream bed).

Since 2000 the Swiss Federal Institute WSL runs an automatic observation station. In 1999 work on a new protection concept began, and from 2010 the municipality of Leuk planned new protection measures.
gained: The check dams hold the channel in place on the fan and protect Susten. The wall of 1967–1969 is now filled with sediment.
The station measures flow height, forces and vibrations of real debris flows, three to five per year on average. The data help to understand debris flows and to test warning systems.
lost: The retention wall is full: its storage space is used up.

The 2012 study notes that letting large debris flows spill into the Pfynwald nature reserve would favour a natural process. That the fixed channel took this process away from the forest is likely but not confirmed.

title: Gondo rockfall wall and the 2000 landslide
place: Gondo, south side of the Simplon Pass
summary: In 2000 a mud and rock flow broke a rockfall protection wall above Gondo; the wall's concrete blocks destroyed part of the village and 13 people died, so the new protection was planned to fail more safely.
why: Gondo is built on old rockfall debris below a high cliff. Because of the danger of falling stones, the municipality built a large rock trap wall above the village in 1988. The wall was made of concrete blocks of about 500 tonnes each.

On 14 October 2000, after 48 hours of heavy rain, about 10,000 m3 of mud and stones slid down and blocked the wall. Water behind it undermined the foundations. Three blocks tipped over, and the flow cut the village in two. Ten buildings, about a third of the village, were destroyed and 13 people died.

The federal event analysis concluded that a protection work can fail and must be planned for this case. For the rebuilding, an earth dam reinforced with steel was chosen instead of the concrete wall, because it does not add destructive blocks when it breaks.
gained: After the disaster a drainage system was built at the foot of the cliff to lead water around the village.
The village and the Stockalper Tower were rebuilt; the tower reopened as a hotel restaurant in 2007.
lost: The wall that should protect against falling stones made the slide much worse. The analysis says protection against one hazard raised the danger from another.

title: Avalanche winter 1999: a test for fifty years of protection

title: Glyssibach and Trachtbach works after the 2005 debris flows
summary: After debris flows killed two people in Brienz in August 2005, the municipalities built a diversion structure and dam on the Glyssibach and a 21 m wide corridor through the village, and a retention barrier on the Trachtbach.
why: On 22 and 23 August 2005 heavy rain caused landslides in the catchments of the Glyssibach and the Trachtbach. Debris flows covered parts of Brienz. A mother and her daughter died in their sleep. Eight houses were swept away and 13 were destroyed.

Brienz, Schwanden and Hofstetten made a protection concept based on 'hold back and let through'. Work on the Glyssibach started in February 2009. High above Brienz a diversion structure leads large debris into a new retention dam. In the village a 21 m wide corridor gives the debris room. On the Trachtbach a retention barrier and ring nets hold back part of the debris.
The works were opened in August 2013. They cost about 43 million francs, paid by the municipalities with help from Bund and canton.
gained: The project was approved without any objection, which the canton's building director called unique.
After 2005 Bund and canton invested about 450 million francs in 50 projects in the canton of Bern. The canton says repeated heavy rains since then did not cause widespread damage.
lost: Several families gave up their houses so that the stream bed could be wider. Not all residents could rebuild at the same place.
In August 2024 the nearby Milibach flooded Brienz again and caused 25 to 30 million francs of damage. Experts asked whether protection works are high enough for a changing climate.

title: Bondo debris-flow basin and protection works
place: Bondo, Bregaglia, at the mouth of the Val Bondasca
summary: After rockfalls at Piz Cengalo, Bondo built a large catch basin and an alarm system, and after the 2017 rock avalanche it built higher walls, new bridges and a bigger dam.
why: In 2011 a rockfall at Piz Cengalo left about 1.5 million m3 of debris at the foot of the mountain. In the next summer, debris flows (fast flows of mud, stones and water) reached Bondo at times. A hazard study showed a high risk of new events. From 2012 to 2016 the authorities built a large catch basin and an alarm system that closes roads automatically.

On 23 August 2017 about 3 million m3 of rock fell from the north face of Piz Cengalo. Eight hikers died. Debris flows of about 500,000 m3 reached Bondo. They filled the retention basin and damaged many buildings. The alarm worked, and the people in the village were evacuated in time.

From 2021 the municipality of Bregaglia rebuilt the protection. After four years of work, higher walls and bridges along the Bondasca and the Mera and a bigger dam at the basin were opened in September 2025.
gained: Without the basin built after 2011, the 2017 debris flows would have done more harm. The national risk report says the warning system let the residents leave in time.
The new works reuse stones that the rock avalanche left in the bed of the Bondasca.
lost: A campsite had to make room for the catch basin.
The works cost 52 million francs. The municipality pays 14 million, Confederation and canton pay a part, and donations pay a large part.

title: Drainage tunnel under the Brienz/Brinzauls landslide
summary: Under the moving village of Brienz/Brinzauls the canton and municipality are building a drainage tunnel of about 2.2 km that takes water out of the landslide to slow it down.
why: Brienz/Brinzauls stands on one of the largest and most active landslides in the Alps. The slide became much faster after 2010. In 2022 the village moved about 135 cm per year, and buildings and roads were badly damaged.

An exploratory tunnel in stable rock below the slide showed that drainage lowers the water pressure and slows the slide. In 2023 the government approved its extension to a drainage tunnel of about 2.2 km. The aim is less than 10 cm movement per year in the village. Bund and canton pay 90 percent of 39.8 million francs.

In summer 2023 a debris stream just missed the village. Because of the danger of a rock fall, the village was evacuated again for more than 60 weeks. In May 2026 almost 80 percent of the tunnel was built. It should be finished at the end of 2027.
gained: From the tunnel, 36 drainage holes take about 850 litres of water per minute out of the ground. The water table in the slide fell by more than 50 m in some areas.
In the village most speeds are now below 5 cm per year. Two years earlier the village moved about 2.5 m per year.
lost: The village is still in a red hazard zone. The municipality plans a preventive resettlement, so the village will change strongly.
The drains may need renewal later. The project leader calls it a task for coming generations.

title: Sihl flood relief tunnel
place: Langnau am Albis to Thalwil, under the Zimmerberg
summary: The canton of Zurich built a 2 km tunnel that takes flood peaks of the Sihl into Lake Zurich, to protect the lower Sihl valley and the city of Zurich.
why: The Sihl is usually a calm river. In extreme storms it can flood the lower Sihl valley and the city of Zurich. Above about 300 m3 per second (cubic metres per second) the river becomes critical for Zurich. In August 2005 the peak was 290 m3 per second.

Several studies found that a relief tunnel was the best solution. The tunnel starts on the Sihl above Langnau am Albis, runs under the Gattikon forest pond through the Zimmerberg hill and ends in Lake Zurich at Thalwil. It is about 2 km long and 6.6 m wide inside. Water flows into it when the Sihl carries more than 250 m3 per second. It can take about 330 m3 per second.

Work started in March 2022. The tunnel boring machine reached Thalwil on 26 November 2024. In August 2026 the last part, a concrete channel about 90 m long into the lake, was under construction. The canton expects the tunnel to be ready in early 2027.
gained: The tunnel protects against a Sihl flood peak of up to 600 m3 per second, an extreme flood with a chance of about once in 500 years.
In an extreme flood, damage in the city of Zurich alone could reach 6.7 billion francs. The canton says the cost of about 175 million francs is small compared to this.
lost: The inlet structure covers a section of the natural Sihl bank. The outlet structure cuts into underwater habitats of Lake Zurich. The canton must replace this nature at Langnau and at Richterswil.
The outlet was built at the site of the Bürger I lake bath in Thalwil. Only the diving tower of the bath was left during the works. Whether the bath will come back is not confirmed.
